provenance.positions: Airport reference point, runway threshold coordinates, elevations and displaced thresholds from the OurAirports open dataset (airports.csv, runways.csv). Navaid positions and frequencies from OurAirports navaids.csv.
notes: All bearings in this file are TRUE. magVarDeg is 0 because magnetic declination over London is currently within about a degree of zero, so true and magnetic headings are treated as interchangeable for gameplay. The VOR slaved variations in the source dataset (about 2.1 to 2.3 degrees west) reflect older calibration epochs and are deliberately not used.

bearingTrue is the published rounded value. The bearing computed geometrically between the 09L and 27R thresholds is about 269.7 degrees; airport.test.ts asserts the two agree within half a degree, so a genuinely wrong threshold or bearing in any future airport file fails the test.

Hold inbound tracks are not published in the source dataset. The loader derives each hold's inbound leg as the bearing from the fix to the airport reference point, which is a sensible default rather than a charted procedure. Override per fix with hold.inboundTrue when real STAR data is added.
Transition altitude is deliberately not encoded: the UK value has been under review and the simulation does not use it yet.
Runway threshold separation between 27R and 27L computes to 0.764 NM (1415 m), matching Heathrow's published parallel centreline spacing.
Surrounding airports and VOR positions are from the same OurAirports datasets. Fifteen aerodromes within about 40 NM and thirteen VOR/VOR-DME within 45 NM are included.

Aerodrome Traffic Zones are computed from the UK rule rather than guessed: radius 2 NM where the longest runway is 1850 m or less and 2.5 NM otherwise, extending to 2000 ft above aerodrome level. They carry derivation "rule" and approximate false.
render.runwayExaggeration is a display-only magnification of the painted runway strip, applied from the threshold so approach geometry stays exact, and faded out as the scope zooms in.

Airspace boundaries come from the VATSIM UK Sector File and are drawn as LINE WORK, not closed polygons. That is what the source is: each record is an independent boundary line, and only 2 of 60 regions chained into a closed ring. Closing them would have invented false edges of up to 30 NM, so regions are stored as one or more open polylines and stroked without closure. A consequence is that these volumes cannot answer "is this aircraft inside the zone" -- containment tests would need ordered closed rings, which is separate work.

Traffic zones for aerodromes the sector file does not cover are still computed from the UK rule and carry derivation "rule". Where the source does publish one, it wins: Biggin Hill is notified as 2.5 NM, whereas the runway-length rule would have given 2 NM. That disagreement is exactly why the published data is preferred.

verticalSource records where each volume vertical extent came from: "file" straight from the sector file header, "rule" for ATZ tops at 2000 ft above aerodrome level, "assumed" where the source header omitted limits (London City CTA, both Gatwick volumes, and the Odiham MATZ).
traffic.seed makes the arrival stream reproducible: the same seed and the same tick count give the same aircraft, which is what allows a scenario to be repeated and a bug report to be acted on.

Entry altitude bands per hold, the fleet mix weights, each operator fleet, the flight number bands and everything under traffic are GAMEPLAY values, not published data. The operator fleets and number bands are plausible rather than authoritative: they exist so the generator cannot produce an easyJet A380 or a Emirates A319, which is the kind of detail that breaks the illusion faster than anything else.
Aircraft types use ICAO designators. Note A359 for the A350-900: there is no designator "A350". A20N and A21N are the neo variants, which are most of the narrowbody arrivals at Heathrow now.

Coastline from the Natural Earth 10m coastline dataset (public domain), clipped to a box roughly 180 NM around the field, simplified with Douglas-Peucker to a 0.1 NM tolerance, then split into chunks spanning at most 12 NM so the renderer can reject an off-screen chunk on its bounding box. Checked against known coastal points: Brighton 0.02 NM, Southend 0.04 NM, Dover 0.20 NM, Harwich 0.24 NM, Beachy Head 0.61 NM from the drawn line.

The London FIR boundary is from the VATSIM UK Sector File, ARTCC/High/EGTT London FIR.txt. Its 39 published segments chain into a single closed ring, so unlike the TMA line work it is continuous; only the portion inside the same box is kept. Long straight legs carry added colinear points, purely so the chunking has somewhere to cut -- the drawn line is unchanged. The Scottish FIR boundary is about 215 NM north of the field and so is absent.

traffic cadence is one arrival every 30 to 60 seconds, ramping from the slower end to the faster over rampMinutes. The interval is clamped to that band so jitter cannot push it outside. entrySpeedKts is the standard entry groundspeed, capped by the type cruise and by the sector speed limit below the limit altitude.

The River Thames is from the VATSIM UK Sector File, Misc Geo/Rivers.txt. That file is an unlabelled pile of 4438 segments -- every line ends in the colour name "river" and nothing identifies the watercourse -- so the segments were chained on shared endpoints into 35 polylines and the Thames was identified by geometry: exactly one chain passes within a mile of Windsor, Richmond, Westminster, Tower Bridge, Woolwich and Gravesend. The per-point widths in metres are APPROXIMATE, interpolated along the line from a table of real widths at fifteen known places (25 m at Oxford to 5 km off Canvey); the source carries no width at all.

The aerodrome list was extended outwards from the original fifteen within 40 NM: every large airport within 100 NM and every medium one within 90 NM that OurAirports records a runway for, which adds twenty-five fields including London Southend, Southampton, Bournemouth, Cambridge, Birmingham and Bristol. Small aerodromes were deliberately left alone -- the close-in strips were curated by hand and there are hundreds of farm strips at that size. Each runway bearing is computed from the two published threshold coordinates rather than taken from the heading column, which is often blank and sometimes magnetic.
